title: PAROXYSMAL EXTREME PAIN DISORDER
alt_titles: PAIN, SUBMANDIBULAR, OCULAR, AND RECTAL, WITH FLUSHING

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEXPD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN9A gene, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Na(v)1.7.

paragraphs.text: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEPD) is an inherited condition characterized by paroxysms of rectal, ocular, or submandibular pain with flushing (Fertleman et al., 2006). Onset is in the neonatal period or infancy and the disorder persists throughout life. Autonomic manifestations, including skin flushing, harlequin color change, tonic attacks, and syncope with bradycardia, predominate early, and attacks of excruciating deep burning pain occur later (Fertleman et al., 2007). The disorder is a sodium channelopathy and is allelic to primary erythermalgia, which has a different biophysical mechanism (Fertleman et al., 2006).

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2007) described the clinical phenotype in 77 individuals from 15 families identified by an international consortium. Fourteen affected individuals completed a validated pain questionnaire. Onset was in the neonatal period or infancy, and the disorder persisted throughout life. Autonomic manifestations predominated at first: all patients had skin flushing, and most had harlequin color change and tonic attacks. Dramatic syncopes with bradycardia, sometimes with asystole, were common. Later, the disorder was characterized by attacks of excruciating deep burning pain, often in the rectal, ocular, or jaw areas, but sometimes diffuse. Triggers included defecation, cold wind, eating, and emotion. Fertleman et al. (2007) noted that the disorder is most likely to be misdiagnosed as epilepsy and, particularly in infancy, as hyperekplexia or reflex anoxic seizures.

paragraphs.text: After a genome-wide linkage search, Fertleman et al. (2006) analyzed the candidate gene SCN9A and identified 8 missense mutations in 11 families and 2 sporadic cases with PEPD. In vitro functional analysis of 3 of the mutant Na(v)1.7 channels showed reduced fast inactivation, which led to a persistent sodium current. Other SCN9A mutations, which shift the activation threshold to more negative values, cause primary erythermalgia. Carbamazepine, which is effective in PEPD but not in primary erythermalgia, selectively blocked the persistent current of the PEPD mutants. It did not affect the negative activation threshold of a primary erythermalgia mutant. Fertleman et al. (2006) concluded that PEPD and primary erythermalgia are allelic disorders with distinct biophysical mechanisms.

paragraphs.text: In a 3-year-old girl with PEPD who had had painful micturition since birth, Meglič et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.554G-A mutation in the SCN9A gene, resulting in an arg185-to-his (R185H) substitution. The mutation was inherited from her father, who had mild symptoms. The authors noted that the same mutation had been found in patients with small fiber sensory neuropathy. They suggested that the intra- and interfamilial phenotypic variability reported for gain-of-function Na(v)1.7 variants could explain this discrepancy.
